I will stay with the cropping pattern I know best in Quzhou: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. Here, that is the safest way for me to keep grain output steady, use my machinery well, and avoid taking market and management risks I do not need. I am 55, and I want a plan I can execute cleanly without depending on complicated new techniques. Wheat gives me a stable summer harvest, and maize fits right after it. This matches the local season, the local soil, and the way water is usually managed here.

Because water is always a constraint on the North China Plain, I will not chase extreme yield by pouring on too much fertilizer or too many irrigations. I will use good seed, but I will keep inputs controlled. For wheat, I will use improved seed, rotary tillage after the maize stubble is handled, base fertilizer plus topdressing, and about 2 irrigations if conditions are normal. I will watch aphids, rust, and later diseases, but I will not spray unless I need to; in a normal year I expect about 2 pesticide passes. For maize, I will sow as soon as wheat is off, use hybrid seed, go with no-tillage to save time and moisture, put most fertilizer in a simple practical program, and rely mainly on rainfall with 1 extra irrigation if needed. I will control weeds early and then watch for armyworm and corn borer. My goal is stable, manageable production, not the highest possible experimental yield.
